baer-heitev/1:א: At the end. That is, tzeit ha'kochavim. Bach, Magen Avraham.
biur-halacha/1:ב: Not later — and therefore one must kindle immediately after tzeit ha'kochavim; and if so, there is a difficulty for one who is always accustomed to pray Ma'ariv at its time, that is, after tzeit ha'kochavim — how should he act? [Peri Megadim] And behold, to delay the evening prayer because of this is also not worthwhile, for it contains the mitzvah of Keriat Shema which is d'oraisa, and also that the frequent comes first, as the Acharonim wrote; therefore it appears to me that such a person should certainly kindle before Ma'ariv, for many Rishonim hold that l'chatchila one should practice thus, as the Gra brought; and further, even the Tur who wrote "at the end of sunset" is explained nearby that he too holds one may advance until close to half an hour beforehand, and especially if one follows the Rambam's ruling that we kindle with sunset, meaning exactly when the sun is concealed from our eyes — and it is known that his view is that the mitzvah of kindling is only about half an hour or slightly more afterward, and if the time passes one does not kindle again; if so, one who kindles at the time of tzeit ha'kochavim does not fulfill the mitzvah of kindling at all per the Rambam and those who follow him at the time of sunset. And even those who are lenient that one may kindle afterward — that too is only because of a safek according to several poskim; therefore it appears good and correct l'chatchila to kindle before Ma'ariv. See Sha'arei Teshuvah who wrote in the name of Machatzit HaShekel likewise that one who does so has not lost; and according to what we proved, one should practice thus l'chatchila.
eshel-avraham/1:_: Not later. See Ba'er Heitev s.k. 2 what Magen Avraham wrote. And in Shav Yaakov siman 22 he raised another reason: since Ma'ariv's time is the entire night and we are not concerned for forgetfulness; and moreover we see that even in the synagogue, while there is still much time, they kindle before Ma'ariv on erev Shabbat — yet the aforementioned Gaon struck a spark and three wondrous reasons emerge from him. And since the time of Keriat Shema and kindling come together, certainly one must give precedence to Keriat Shema which is d'oraisa; and also that the frequent comes first; see siman 684 that even in rabbinic matters the frequent comes first; and some say that in siman 678 Hanukkah precedes Kiddush because it is possible with bread. See there that he rejects all the reasons with a spirit of the times — certainly one prays before kindling on erev Shabbat.
mishnah-berurah/1:א: (1) With the end of its setting — that is, tzeit ha'kochavim, when people pass by and stop and see in their homes, and there is pirsumei nisa. However on erev Shabbat they advance, as below in siman 679. Behold, the Mechaber ruled anonymously per the Tur and his supporters who hold that what the Gemara said — that the time to kindle the Hanukkah light is from sunset — means the end of sunset; but in truth many Rishonim hold that the Gemara's intent is on the beginning of the second sunset, which is about a quarter hour earlier; see in Biur Halacha what we explained for those who are accustomed to pray Ma'ariv at its time, that is after tzeit ha'kochavim — it is correct l'chatchila to kindle before Ma'ariv; so too in Mor U'Ketzia; and so practiced the Gra [however he should put enough oil that it burns half an hour after tzeit ha'kochavim]. If he did not kindle beforehand and the time of tzeit ha'kochavim arrived, he should give precedence to praying Ma'ariv, for it is frequent and also contains Keriat Shema which is d'oraisa [Sha'arei Teshuvah]. Know that even those always accustomed to kindle after the evening prayer — it is still proper that they at least prepare the oil in the lamps before the evening prayer so it is ready immediately after prayer to kindle; for if he does everything after the evening prayer, there is certainly concern he will pass the main time of kindling, which is half an hour by Gemara law.
peri-megadim/1:א: Perhaps Taz extended and ruled that if one put more oil than the measure even without specification, it is not designated for Hanukkah beyond the half-hour measure. He explained that one who designates for Hanukkah even more than the measure — it is forbidden to benefit from it; so too the Levush in siman 677. But the Bach is stringent in siman 677 even without specification for the first night, for if he did not kindle, one could say the entire oil was designated even without specification on erev Shabbat; Magen Avraham letter 4. Maharshal ruled that while it is burning it is forbidden to use even more than the measure — the viewer, etc.; and there is support from oils kindled for Hanukkah on Shabbat, for it is forbidden to use their light, and presumably one puts more oil than the measure since one cannot limit it, and one should be concerned lest he uses afterward; it teaches that all while burning is forbidden, etc.; it is strained to say he designated explicitly for Hanukkah, for then it would be forbidden to use even after the measure — if so, in what do they disagree with the view that permits using its light? And in siman 673 Taz 5 it implies forbidden to use its light because of bizui mitzvah or the viewer says he kindles for his need — not because it was designated for the mitzvah; it will be explained there. If he put much oil beyond the measure and it went out within the time when a little remains beyond the measure and most is excess — Eliyah Rabbah letter 2 and siman 677; apparently excess oil requires nullification in sixty unlike milk where there is no eating permitted, only benefit — one could say even in bread thus it is nullified in the majority — requires study. It will be explained further in siman 677. And the Rama in chapter 4 seems to rule like both answers stringently: one must kindle specifically within this time, and also must give the half-hour measure; and leniently too that if more than half an hour remains it is permitted; and nevertheless there. We hold as Shulchan Aruch ruled: what requires half an hour — even if it went out, it is forbidden to use its light; see siman 677. See in responsa Chacham Tzvi siman 90 in the name of the Rosh chapter 10 of Pesachim in the name of Rabbeinu Tam to kindle so there is a delay of half an hour; and for the first answer — if he did not kindle it is difficult — one could say the two answers do not contradict and both are true: if he did not kindle, etc., and the measure too that one must put oil in the lamp as measure; see siman 675 seif 2 and Peri Chadash here that measure is required before kindling, and if he blessed without measure he returns, extinguishes, and puts measure — requires study whether he blesses for the first night — one could say measure is not required; and from "we bless to kindle" one could say other explanations; the Mechaber there wrote in the name of some who say, and nevertheless such is the halacha; the Levush wrote anonymously there — it will be explained.
shaarei-teshuvah/2:_: Until it is finished. Eliyah Rabbah wrote in the name of Knesset HaGedolah, etc., to kindle after Ma'ariv; so too in Shevut Yaakov; afterward he brought Magen Avraham's words and in the name of Knesset HaGedolah; one who examines Shevut Yaakov will see Eliyah Rabbah's words are reversed — there he brought Magen Avraham and wrote on this; however in Knesset HaGedolah it is written "and in my choice, etc., I returned to my custom to kindle after the evening prayer," and such is the essential law — certainly the frequent comes first, as one can do both, as Tosafot wrote on Shabbat 23 — see there; see below siman 684 in Magen Avraham and Peri Chadash there; see what Yad Ephraim wrote there; see in Eshel Avraham here in the name of Shav Yaakov on this; see Machatzit HaShekel who showed room for four views in Maharash's conclusion siman 2, and Machatzit HaShekel concluded it seems one who kindles before going to pray Ma'ariv has not lost, for there is concern that until he prays Ma'ariv the kindling time — half an hour by Gemara law — will pass; see there.
turei-zahav/2:_: One may extinguish it, etc. In siman 676 the Tur and Rosh ruled from She'iltot that excess Hanukkah oil one may make a bonfire, etc.; Beit Yosef questioned below from here that one may extinguish after the kindling measure, and answered that there it speaks of what remains of the oil needed for the kindling measure, which was designated for his mitzvah, therefore he makes a bonfire; here it speaks of one who put oil beyond the measure, and after the measure burned it is permitted to benefit, for only the required measure was designated for the mitzvah — such is the truth of this answer. There Beit Yosef brings another answer in the name of Mahari Abuhav: one should distinguish — if he put oil in the lamp without designating except for the kindling time measure, afterward he may use it if he wishes; but if he put oil in the lamp without specification, then it was designated for the Hanukkah mitzvah and he must make a bonfire — end. I find this answer difficult from what is stated in the chapter "the judgment was concluded" for Abbaye, who holds designation is a word — they challenged from what we learned: the dead person's property is permitted to his heirs, thus designation is nothing; they answered Abbaye holds this tanna holds designation is something — if it suits him he seizes it, and what does not suit him he need not take out with it; and Rava who argues there and holds designation is nothing — nevertheless they do not argue on this matter that the prohibition is not seized except for what suits him; for Rava, if one acts with something that is a thing, nevertheless the prohibition is not more stringent than Abbaye for designation alone — if so, we see the prohibition that comes through forbidden benefit to the dead is seized only in what suits him, not in what is permitted; if we were to say that what he designated much oil for Hanukkah became forbidden, etc., we should say the same for the dead's permitted property — but certainly the prohibition is only in what is needed for Hanukkah. Granted for Beit Yosef's answer there is no prohibition except in what remains of the required measure, that is, it went out and he need not relight — we still say it is forbidden because it was designated for Hanukkah in what he needs. It is also wondrous where to learn prohibition here in what is not needed for Hanukkah — not from the answer that answers the matter "from sunset until the market clears," meaning the measure Rif and Rosh explain one must put oil so it burns that measure; if it kept burning until that measure and he wants to extinguish or use its light, permission is in his hand — it implies explicitly there is no prohibition in excess beyond the measure; if you would say this speaks where he explains he designates only what is needed for the measure, obviously there is no other tanna — but certainly we say so anonymously, and even for the first answer that if he did not kindle he kindles — nevertheless it does not speak at all of the permitted case; from where do we forbid? On the contrary, it seems comparable to permitted property of the dead we mentioned; but if it went out before its time, we may say the remainder is forbidden because of designation for the mitzvah — from this She'iltot speaks, and explicitly Ran wrote: but some Geonim said if it went out and oil remained in the lamp on the first day, he kindles on the second day, etc. — that is the She'iltot we mentioned; it teaches specifically when it went out She'iltot and the Geonim speak, but Ran is difficult — for before that he wrote Rif does not hold thus, for it appears from his words that if it went out it is permitted to use the oil, and so too he, and the reason: because he did not designate it except for the mitzvah, that is, all while it burns within mitzvah time — if it went out it is permitted, similar to sukkah wood after the festival which is permitted — end. From making a dispute between Rif and the Geonim it implies he does not distinguish like Beit Yosef's distinction, and holds whoever permits extinguishing after the measure automatically permits benefiting from them; likewise if it went out by itself within the measure it is permitted to benefit, for that too is called after the measure since one need not relight — there is no designation for the mitzvah; but Rosh and Tur distinguish as Beit Yosef wrote, and they did not need to mention the distinction, for anonymously it implies thus — for here they wrote permission only if he put more than the measure, and in siman 677 they wrote the remainder of the oil, etc., implying the remainder of the measure that he presumably put there as measure — therefore Shulchan Aruch ruled well that one may extinguish after the measure; so too Maharshal in his summary of Hanukkah laws in his responsa, only he noted there it is forbidden to use its light if he did not extinguish because of the viewer — meaning the viewer thinks even within the measure it is permitted to use its light, but after extinguishing it is permitted to benefit from them if they already burned the measure; he too distinguished like Beit Yosef: "and that which we ruled above after he kindled his measure it is permitted to extinguish and do as he wishes — that is revealing the matter retroactively that he put more than the measure; but where he put only the measure and it went out, or the wick was bad and sputtering in such a case it is forbidden" — end; such is essential, and the stringency Beit Yosef wrote in the name of Mahari Abuhav does not appear to be halacha for the reason we said. Maharshal also wrote: immediately when his time begins he should not eat or study until he kindles; if he began he stops; if he delayed the time, even though he did the mitzvah improperly, nevertheless his time is until chatzot when there is still pirsumei nisa; but to advance is not possible at all on erev Shabbat; and the prayer leader who kindles in the synagogue on erev Shabbat kindles before Minchah — end.
